summary:
Huánuco stands under Peru's national framework: Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

The restriction on facilities is national in scope. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting any person from entering public sanitary facilities designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions for custody and for cases where required, including accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities, and obliging venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. The text still required plenary backing at that point, and the reported trigger was a July 2023 complaint over gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport. Activist Gianna Camacho argued the measure is discriminatory and that enforcement would rest on security staff checking the DNI to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender.

The plenary then acted on 2 April 2025, approving and waiving a second vote on the dictamen of the Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes, whose Article 5.1 prohibits persons from entering or using public sanitary facilities designated for a sex other than their birth sex. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, analysing the provision on 15 April 2025 with Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors. IDEHPUCP finds the provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people, implicitly framing them as harassment risks, and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Enforcement reaches private and public life. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy, in SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. The annual report of the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia, cited by Agencia Presentes on 22 July 2024, records 54 assassinations of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases across 2020-2023, the homicide victims being 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian. Nineteen killings occurred in 2023 alone, twelve of them trans women, and the killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of the 19 in 2023. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

Individual cases are on the record. In February 2023 trans sex worker Rubi Torres Silvano, 31, was kidnapped from central Lima by a 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and killed in Carabayllo with some 30 gunshots, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco, 30, was shot; two killers were arrested in March 2023. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

None of the sources covering these measures contains Huánuco-specific content, so the department is assessed on the national position.
tangentialFactors:
The state's own protective baseline is weaker than the Inter-American standard. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

The 2024 report drawing on the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected, and its co-author Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such.

Public speech has been used to enforce the facility restriction. The dehumanising comparisons recorded on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu and the on-air instruction to Susel Paredes to 'go use the men's room' show the policy travelling beyond statutes into broadcast and parliamentary rhetoric.
localsOnly:
For residents, gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, which bears directly on whether a person can present documents matching their lived gender when restroom access is policed by identity papers.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are also constrained for residents. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people. The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.
outOfScopeNotes:
The three source documents examined here contain no Huánuco-specific reporting: the Infobae, IDEHPUCP and Agencia Presentes pieces address the national statute, the national institute's legal analysis and nationwide tallies. Whether the facility restriction has been enforced in Huánuco by venue staff, municipal authorities or police is not sourced and remains unresolved.

The violence figures are national totals for 2020-2023 with no departmental breakdown, and the source's own author describes the count as a sub-registry; the true number of killings and rights violations in Huánuco is not established by these materials.

The claim that hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such follows from the absence of sexual orientation and gender identity from the state's crime-registration systems, but no source documents how that gap has played out in Huánuco prosecutions, and no department-level case data is available to verify enforcement patterns.
